quizName: DMV Practice Test #14 25 Questions • Passing Score 21

questions.question: Most motorcycle crashes happen:

options.text: At speeds over 55 mph.
After riding for several hours.
On short trips.
On long trips.

questions.correctAnswerText: On short trips.
questions.explanation: Most motorcycle crashes happen on trips shorter than 5 miles at speeds under 30 mph.

questions.question: When riding a motorcycle, you should:

options.text: Stay in one part of the lane and never move from it.
Change your lane position based on road and traffic conditions.
Ride in the center of the lane so other vehicles see you better.
Ride in a zigzag pattern so drivers notice you.

questions.correctAnswerText: Change your lane position based on road and traffic conditions.
questions.explanation: There is no single best lane position. Change your position as needed based on the road and traffic conditions around you.

questions.question: To swerve, you should:

options.text: Turn the handlebars quickly.
Shift your weight quickly.
Press the handgrip toward the direction you want to turn.
Press the handgrip away from the direction you want to turn.

questions.correctAnswerText: Press the handgrip toward the direction you want to turn.
questions.explanation: To swerve, press the handgrip on the side where you want to go. To swerve left, press the left handgrip, then press the right to straighten. To swerve right, press the right handgrip, then the left.

questions.question: Riding on the far side of a lane when following another vehicle:

options.text: Is recommended because you will be seen easily.
Is not recommended because drivers rarely check their side mirrors.
Is recommended because a passenger may tell the driver you are there.
Is illegal because you must ride in the center of the lane.

questions.correctAnswerText: Is not recommended because drivers rarely check their side mirrors.
questions.explanation: Most drivers look at their rearview mirror more than their side mirrors. When following a car, ride in the center of the lane where the driver is most likely to see you in the rearview mirror.

questions.question: When being passed from behind, you should:

options.text: Move onto the shoulder.
Use the left portion of your lane.
Use the center portion of your lane.
Use the right portion of your lane.

questions.correctAnswerText: Use the center portion of your lane.
questions.explanation: The center portion of the lane is safest when being passed. Riding on the side near the passing vehicle risks a collision. Riding on the far side may cause the driver to return to your lane unsafely.

questions.question: If you brake while turning:

options.text: Use only the front brake.
It works the same as braking on a straight road.
You will have more traction as you lean into the turn.
You may have less traction as you lean into the turn.

questions.correctAnswerText: You may have less traction as you lean into the turn.
questions.explanation: You can use both brakes while turning, but it requires care. Some of your tire's traction is used for turning while leaning, so less traction is available for stopping.

questions.question: When loading cargo on a motorcycle, you should:

options.text: Pack heavier items in front of the tank bag.
Pack lighter items near the front.
Avoid placing items over the rear axle.
Place items behind the rear axle.

questions.correctAnswerText: Pack heavier items in front of the tank bag.
questions.explanation: Pack heavier items in front of the tank bag. Load weight over or in front of the rear axle. Putting weight behind the rear axle can affect your control.

questions.question: What does this hand signal mean?

options.text: Slow or stop
Left turn
Right turn
Backing up

questions.correctAnswerText: Slow or stop
questions.explanation: A bent left arm pointing downward means the rider plans to slow down or stop. Hand signals can be used instead of or along with turn signals.

questions.question: When riding in a group, inexperienced riders should be placed:

options.text: In the front of the group.
Just behind the lead rider.
At the back of the group.
Anywhere within the group.

questions.correctAnswerText: Just behind the lead rider.
questions.explanation: Inexperienced riders should ride near the front of the group, just behind the leader. This allows experienced riders to watch them from behind.

questions.question: Each traffic lane gives a motorcyclist how many paths of travel?

options.text: One
Two
Three
Four

questions.correctAnswerText: Three
questions.explanation: Each traffic lane has three paths of travel for motorcyclists: the left, center, and right portions.

questions.question: Do you need hearing protection on a motorcycle?

options.text: No, a helmet is enough.
Yes, you need it in addition to a helmet.
Only on windy days.
No, not if you carry a passenger.

questions.correctAnswerText: Yes, you need it in addition to a helmet.
questions.explanation: Engine and wind noise can damage your hearing, even when wearing a helmet. Hearing protection helps prevent this damage while still letting you hear important sounds like horns and sirens.

questions.question: What does a linked braking system do?

options.text: It connects the front and rear brakes. When you use either brake lever, both brakes apply.
It connects the front brake to the gear shifter and applies the brake when you downshift.
It connects the rear brake to a foot control.
It connects the rear brake to a handlebar switch.

questions.correctAnswerText: It connects the front and rear brakes. When you use either brake lever, both brakes apply.
questions.explanation: A linked braking system connects the front and rear brakes. Using either the front or rear brake lever applies braking pressure to both brakes. Check your owner's manual for details about your motorcycle's braking system.

questions.question: If you need to brake and swerve to avoid a hazard, what should you do?

options.text: Do one action, then the other.
Do both at the same time.
Always brake first, then swerve.
Try to use only the brakes.

questions.correctAnswerText: Do one action, then the other.
questions.explanation: Perform braking and swerving as separate actions. You can brake then swerve, or swerve then brake. Never do both at the same time.

questions.question: Is the oily strip in the center of a lane safe for motorcyclists?

options.text: No, never.
Yes, usually, unless the road is wet.
Yes, usually, unless it is sunny.
Yes, always, in any weather.

questions.correctAnswerText: Yes, usually, unless the road is wet.
questions.explanation: Oil from cars collects in a strip down the center of lanes. On dry roads, this strip usually has enough grip for safe riding. On wet roads, it becomes slippery. The strip is usually about two feet wide, so you can often ride beside it while staying in the center portion of the lane.

questions.question: What should you do if your front wheel starts to skid?

options.text: Keep the front brake engaged and ride out the skid.
Keep the front brake engaged and release the rear brake.
Release the front brake immediately, then apply it again smoothly.
Release the front brake and press harder on the rear brake.

questions.correctAnswerText: Release the front brake immediately, then apply it again smoothly.
questions.explanation: If your front wheel locks while braking, release the front brake completely right away. Then apply it again gently.

questions.question: When carrying a passenger, which of these do you NOT need to adjust?

options.text: Tire pressure.
Mirror positions.
Headlight position.
Brake light position.

questions.correctAnswerText: Brake light position.
questions.explanation: A passenger adds weight, which changes how the motorcycle sits. You may need to adjust tire pressure, suspension, shocks, headlight, and mirrors. You do not need to adjust the brake light position.

questions.question: When planning a long group ride, which idea should you NOT use?

options.text: Plan travel distances based on the least experienced rider.
Skip breaks to reach your destination faster.
Place inexperienced riders behind the leaders.
Ride in a staggered formation.

questions.correctAnswerText: Skip breaks to reach your destination faster.
questions.explanation: Plan routes based on the least experienced rider's skill level. Take regular breaks to reduce fatigue. Place new riders behind leaders so experienced riders can watch them. Ride in a staggered formation for safety.

questions.question: A small animal enters your lane while you are riding in traffic. What should you do?

options.text: Swerve into other lanes to avoid the animal.
Switch lanes as quickly as possible.
Stay in your lane.
Flash your lights to scare the animal.

questions.correctAnswerText: Stay in your lane.
questions.explanation: While you should try to avoid hitting an animal, staying in your lane is most important in traffic. Swerving into another lane risks hitting another vehicle. Hitting a small animal is safer than hitting another vehicle.

questions.question: A vehicle is passing you on your left. Where should you ride in your lane?

options.text: Move as far right as possible.
Move to the shoulder.
Ride in the center of your lane.
Ride on the left side of your lane.

questions.correctAnswerText: Ride in the center of your lane.
questions.explanation: Ride in the center of your lane when being passed. Riding on the side nearest the passing vehicle increases collision risk. Riding on the far side may encourage the driver to merge back too soon. Stay centered.

questions.question: When it is raining, where should you ride?

options.text: In the center of the lane.
Pull off the road until the rain stops.
In the tire tracks left by cars.
Increase your speed.

questions.correctAnswerText: In the tire tracks left by cars.
questions.explanation: Wet pavement is very slippery when rain first starts. Oil from cars has not yet washed away. Ride in the tire tracks left by cars for better grip. The left tire track is often your best choice.

questions.question: If you must swerve, what should you do?

options.text: Shift your weight quickly.
Turn your handlebars quickly.
Press the handgrip in the direction you want to turn.
Press the handgrip in the opposite direction of the turn.

questions.correctAnswerText: Press the handgrip in the direction you want to turn.
questions.explanation: To swerve and avoid a hazard, press the handgrip in the direction you want to go. To swerve left, press the left handgrip, then press the right to straighten. To swerve right, press the right handgrip, then the left.

questions.question: When riding in a group, what does it mean when the lead rider raises their left arm with their index finger extended?

options.text: Speed up.
Slow down.
Form a single-file line.
The group will exit soon.

questions.correctAnswerText: Form a single-file line.
questions.explanation: Hand signals help riders in a group communicate. When the lead rider raises their left arm and extends their index finger, it means the group should move into a single-file formation.

questions.question: When should a passenger get on a motorcycle?

options.text: Before the engine starts.
After the engine starts.
As far back on the seat as possible.
While holding the seat.

questions.correctAnswerText: After the engine starts.
questions.explanation: A passenger should get on the motorcycle only after the engine has started and the transmission is in neutral. The passenger should sit as far forward as possible without blocking the driver's control. The passenger should hold onto the driver's waist, hips, or belt.

questions.question: What helps you ride safely on slippery surfaces?

options.text: Using only the front brake.
Using both brakes.
Using the center lane.
Keeping your speed the same or going faster.

questions.correctAnswerText: Using both brakes.
questions.explanation: On slippery surfaces, slow down and use both brakes. Avoid sudden movements. Stay out of the center lane and follow the tire tracks left by cars. Watch for hazards like oil spots and loose gravel.

questions.question: Which statement is true?

options.text: The front and rear brakes have equal stopping power.
The front brake is more powerful than the rear brake.
The rear brake is more powerful than the front brake.
Use only the front brake when stopping.

questions.correctAnswerText: The front brake is more powerful than the rear brake.
questions.explanation: The front brake provides most of a motorcycle's stopping power—at least 70 percent. Always use both brakes when you slow down or stop.
